what: Build Check Part 1 (ROC Operations Manual §14.2A): every source the Source Register lists for a finding was reopened on 7 October 2026 and each recorded quotation looked for on its page. 'also_says' lists further sentences the checkers confirmed on the same pages. Two pages (HSOC-AUG, HSOC-AUT) returned a server error on every try, including a later try.

read_again_by_the_builder.sentence: Remove all leaves from bushes and rake up all around the rose beds.
spray on bare roses and lightly on ground around bushes to kill all black spot spores
Frost hollows often occur in valleys due to cold air drainage.
This is referred to as a katabatic wind, and can result in frost forming in valleys when surrounding areas remain frost-free.
Use [brand] and White Oil mixed together to spray on bare roses and lightly on ground around bushes to kill all black spot spores.

checks.recorded: If you live near the coast, and rarely or never get frosts, the most dormant period is late June to the end of July.
checks.page_wording: If you live near the coast, and rarely or never get frosts, the most dormant period is late June to the end of July.
checks.note: Page (NSW society) splits pruning by coast with no frosts versus inland or regular frosts, so it supports timing by frost/coast. It says nothing about the five gardening zones, so the 'not by zones' part is not shown by this page alone. NSW.

checks.recorded: If you live near the coast, and rarely or never get frosts, the most dormant period is late June to the end of July.
checks.page_wording: If you live near the coast, and rarely or never get frosts, the most dormant period is late June to the end of July.
checks.note: Supports late June to end of July for main pruning on the NSW coast with no/rare frost. The page does not say early July is ideal (asked twice; not stated). Publisher is NSW; sentence names coastal, rarely frosty areas.

checks.recorded: it is best to prune from the beginning to the end of August.
checks.page_wording: If you live inland or an area that gets any frosts over a regular period, it is best to prune from the beginning to the end of August.
checks.note: Supports August main pruning for NSW inland or regularly frosty areas. Victoria, South Australia and Canberra are not named on this page (NSW society, no other place stated).

checks.recorded: The best time to prune roses is when they are in their most dormant period.
checks.page_wording: The best time to prune roses is when they are in their most dormant period.
checks.note: Page ties pruning to dormancy and region/frost months, with no mention of bud swell found. Fits the finding that this page does not use bud swell. NSW, no other place stated.

checks.recorded: First feed after the winter prune
checks.page_wording: First feed after the winter prune; second feed in mid September in time in the warmer zones or early to mid-October in the cooler zones; third feed...
checks.note: First feed is tied to the winter prune, not a month. NSW society, no region stated for this sentence. Later feeds are given by month.

checks.recorded: second feed in mid September in time in the warmer zones or early to mid-October in the cooler zones
checks.page_wording: second feed in mid September in time in the warmer zones or early to mid-October in the cooler zones
checks.note: This is the SECOND feed, mid-September warmer vs early-to-mid October cooler zones, about 2-4 weeks later; it is not the spring start of feeding. Zones are not defined. NSW society.

checks.recorded: the last feed in mid to late February.
checks.page_wording: ...and the last feed in mid to late February.
checks.note: Supports last feed mid to late February. Finding says late summer to early autumn, February to March, southern states; page gives only mid-late February, written by NSW society, no other place stated.

checks.recorded: Bare rooted plants are dormant – they have no leaves or flowers and are only available in winter.
checks.page_wording: Bare rooted plants are dormant – they have no leaves or flowers and are only available in winter.
checks.note: Says bare-root roses are only available in winter; gives no June/July planting months (asked directly). NSW, no place stated.

checks.recorded: Roses growing in pots are available for sale all year round
checks.page_wording: Roses growing in pots are available for sale all year round and are actively growing with leaves and possibly flowers.
checks.note: Says potted roses are for sale all year; does not say they can be planted any time or to avoid hot weather (asked; no such sentence). NSW only; South Australia not on page.

also_says.quote: If you live inland or an area that gets any frosts over a regular period, it is best to prune from the beginning to the end of August.
also_says.note: Main winter pruning, August, NSW inland or regular frost areas

also_says.quote: Clean up all the prunings, pick off any foliage and clear up dead and diseased leaves from the garden.
also_says.note: Clear-up after pruning, no month given, NSW society; no spray type named on page

checks.recorded: In cold areas it is better not to prune until August.
checks.page_wording: In cold areas it is better not to prune until August.
checks.note: July section, main pruning, Rose Society of NSW; 'cold areas' versus 'mild areas', so frost/climate wording not zones. Does not itself mention the five gardening zones or coast/inland. No place stated beyond NSW publisher.

checks.recorded: [No definition of mild, cold, cool or warm areas on the page; checked directly.]
checks.note: Asked directly; page gives no definition of mild, cold, cool or warm areas. Page uses 'mild', 'cold', 'cool', 'warm' areas undefined. NSW society.

checks.recorded: In mild areas this is the ideal month for pruning roses. [July]
checks.page_wording: In mild areas this is the ideal month for pruning roses.
checks.note: July section: July is ideal for main pruning in 'mild areas' (undefined). Does not say coastal or frost-free, nor 'late June'. NSW society, no place stated beyond that.

checks.recorded: In cold areas it is better not to prune until August.
checks.page_wording: In cold areas it is better not to prune until August.
checks.note: Supports delaying main pruning to August in 'cold areas' (undefined); does not say frosty or inland, nor name Victoria, South Australia or Canberra. NSW society.

checks.recorded: Young growth in those areas is very subject to damage by frosts.
checks.page_wording: Young growth in those areas is very subject to damage by frosts.
checks.note: Follows the cold-areas sentence in the July section; gives frost damage to young growth as the reason for waiting until August. NSW society.

checks.recorded: The latter half of August is ideal for feeding roses
checks.page_wording: The latter half of August is ideal for feeding roses, though in cold areas this can be delayed until September.
checks.note: August section: spring feeding in latter half of August, with September in cold areas. Supports 'late August or September' but only for this NSW society; no other state named.

checks.recorded: though in cold areas this can be delayed until September.
checks.page_wording: The latter half of August is ideal for feeding roses, though in cold areas this can be delayed until September.
checks.note: Supports delay of spring feeding in cold areas to September, from latter half of August. It gives no 'two to four weeks' figure; cold areas undefined. NSW society.

checks.recorded: trim your plants early this month in mild climate areas. In cool areas do this in January
checks.page_wording: trim your plants early this month in mild climate areas. In cool areas do this in January for March blooms
checks.note: February section: light trim to time autumn blooms, January to March by area. NSW society, areas undefined.

checks.recorded: in warm areas trim in March for blooms in May.
checks.page_wording: In cool areas do this in January for March blooms, and in warm areas trim in March for blooms in May.
checks.note: Matches: January cool, early February mild, March warm. Summer trim for autumn flowers. NSW society; areas undefined.

checks.recorded: those growing in March and April will mature adequately before mid-winter.
checks.page_wording: Stake all basal shoots; those growing in March and April will mature adequately before mid-winter.
checks.note: March section, NSW society. Says shoots growing in March and April mature before mid-winter. No region stated.

checks.recorded: Prepare the soil for planting in June/July.
checks.page_wording: Prepare the soil for planting in June/July.
checks.note: Under the Late April/May heading; it says to prepare soil for planting in June/July, not that planting is in those months, and does not say bare-root. A separate sentence about soaking bare-root roses sits under a planting month (page appears to say June). NSW society.

checks.recorded: Lime Sulphur is recognised as being effective [July]
checks.page_wording: Lime Sulphur is recognised as being effective and it will also address white scale.
checks.note: July section: spray immediately after pruning is finished; page names a fungicide aimed at black spot, mildew and rust, and lime sulphur. Winter spray type: lime sulphur. NSW society (July), no other place stated.

contradictions: The page calls July 'the ideal month' for pruning in mild areas, whereas the NSW Growing Roses page says coastal frost-free pruning is late June to end of July and gives no 'ideal' month.

also_says.quote: Immediately pruning is completed, the prunings and fallen leaves should be put in the green waste bin and the plants sprayed with a fungicide
also_says.note: July, after main pruning; clear-up of leaves and prunings; NSW society, no region stated

also_says.quote: Remove faded flowers.
also_says.note: December section only; the page gives no stop month for deadheading. NSW society

checks.recorded: Start pruning roses. [July]
checks.page_wording: Start pruning roses. Remove all leaves from bushes and rake up all around the rose beds.
checks.note: July section of the Rose Society of Victoria calendar: main pruning starts in July. Page is written for Victoria; no region qualifier on this sentence. Supports July as the pruning month for Victoria only.

checks.recorded: Prune now in cold areas so as to avoid frost damage. [August]
checks.page_wording: Prune now in cold areas so as to avoid frost damage.
checks.note: August section: pruning in cold areas of Victoria is placed in August to avoid frost damage. 'Cold areas' undefined; no mention of inland, South Australia, NSW or Canberra. Wording reads as 'prune now', i.e. prune in August in cold areas.

checks.recorded: At end of month feed all roses with a specialist rose fertiliser [August]
checks.page_wording: At end of month feed all roses with a specialist rose fertiliser, except newly planted bare-root roses ... half the recommended amount.
checks.note: August section, Victoria: feed at the end of August. Supports 'late August' but not 'or September'; no cold-area delay is stated here.

checks.recorded: newly planted bare-root roses which should not be fed until late November or early December
checks.page_wording: except newly planted bare-root roses which should not be fed until late November or early December but at half the recommended amount.
checks.note: August section, Victoria: new bare-root roses not fed until late November or early December. Applies to newly planted bare-root roses only.

checks.recorded: Summer-trim all roses if timing flowering for a show or special event. [February]
checks.page_wording: Summer-trim all roses if timing flowering for a show or special event.
checks.note: February section, Victoria: summer trim is for timing flowers for a show or event. It gives February only, not January to March, and does not mention autumn flowers.

checks.recorded: Deadhead and enjoy. [April]
checks.page_wording: Deadhead and enjoy.
checks.note: Page has 'Deadhead and enjoy.' under April (second check confirmed), also deadheading in Nov, Dec and Jan. No stop month is given; May has no deadheading line found. Supports 'continue into April' only for Victoria, not May.

checks.recorded: Start planting new roses using compost and slow-release fertiliser only. [June]
checks.page_wording: Start planting new roses using compost and slow-release fertiliser only.
checks.note: June section, Victoria: planting starts in June. The page's May entry mentions ordering new roses for winter planting. Not stated as bare-root; no July planting line checked, so 'June and July' only partly shown.

checks.recorded: Move established roses to new locations if they are in the wrong place or too close together. [June]
checks.page_wording: Move established roses to new locations if they are in the wrong place or too close together.
checks.note: June section, Victoria: moving established roses is listed in June. It does not say 'while dormant' or 'winter'; June is a winter month.

checks.recorded: Remove all leaves from bushes and rake up all around the rose beds. [July]
checks.page_wording: Remove all leaves from bushes and rake up all around the rose beds.
checks.note: July section, Victoria, alongside 'Start pruning roses'. Supports clearing at winter pruning in July; August is not mentioned for this.

checks.recorded: spray on bare roses and lightly on ground around bushes to kill all black spot spores [July]
checks.page_wording: ... spray on bare roses and lightly on ground around bushes to kill all black spot spores.
checks.note: July section, Victoria: after pruning, bare roses sprayed. Types named: copper-based fungicide with white oil; alternative lime sulphur.

contradictions: The page puts feeding at the end of August for all roses and no delay to September in cold areas, whereas other sources delay.

also_says.quote: Alternative spray is Lime Sulphur.
also_says.note: July, winter spray on bare roses after pruning; also copper with white oil; Victoria

also_says.quote: Continue deadheading.
also_says.note: January section; Victoria

also_says.quote: order new roses for winter planting
also_says.note: May section, Victoria; planting starts June

checks.recorded: The best time to prune is in June or July.
checks.page_wording: The best time to prune is in June or July.
checks.note: Rose Society of Victoria: main pruning June or July (Victoria; sentence says 'in Australia' only for the cold-area exception). Supports June opening for Victoria only; South Australia, Western Australia and Brisbane are not named.

checks.recorded: if you live in a really cold area of Australia, then wait until early August
checks.page_wording: But if you live in a really cold area of Australia, then wait until early August so that the frosts don't knock back the new shoots.
checks.note: Supports delay to early August for 'a really cold area of Australia' (undefined), main pruning. Does not name inland, frosty, NSW, South Australia or Canberra; says early August, not all of August.

checks.recorded: so that the frosts don't knock back the new shoots.
checks.page_wording: ...wait until early August so that the frosts don't knock back the new shoots.
checks.note: States the reason for delay in really cold areas: frost damage to new shoots. Victorian society; place stated is 'a really cold area of Australia'.

checks.recorded: [No sentence timing pruning by bud swell or new growth; checked directly.]
checks.note: Asked directly twice: no sentence times pruning by bud swell or buds starting to move; page uses months (June/July, early August) and frost. Victorian society.

contradictions: One WebFetch answer said the page advises avoiding winter pruning of repeat-flowering roses before July in most areas; two further asks could only return the June or July sentence, so that claim is unconfirmed and not recorded.

checks.recorded: "It's rose pruning time! Start with climbing roses, followed by bush roses." [July]
checks.page_wording: It's rose pruning time! Start with climbing roses, followed by bush roses.
checks.note: Under the July heading of the Rose Society of South Australia calendar (South Australia; page undated). Supports July as the main winter pruning month for bush roses, for South Australia only; no frost or region split on the page.

checks.recorded: "Fertilise early in the month" [September]
checks.page_wording: Fertilise early in the month with Neutrog Sudden Impact for Roses.
checks.note: Under September heading, South Australia (publisher's state). Supports early September for the spring feed, but not August; the page names a brand product. The finding says late August or September, so only the September half is supported.

checks.recorded: "This is the month to fertilise" [February]
checks.page_wording: This is the month to fertilise with Neutrog Sudden Impact for Roses pellets.
checks.note: Under February heading, South Australia. Supports a February feed, but the page does not call it the last feed, and the finding's March half is not supported by this sentence. Page gives no end-of-feeding statement.

checks.recorded: "Roses can be trimmed in summer, one to two weeks after fertilising, to achieve a strong and vibrant autumn flush."
checks.page_wording: Roses can be trimmed in summer, one to two weeks after fertilising, to achieve a strong and vibrant autumn flush.
checks.note: Under February heading, South Australia. Supports a summer trim timed after the February feed for autumn flowers; it gives no January-to-March range and no 'light' qualifier in this sentence.

checks.recorded: "Ensure rose prunings and as many fallen leaves as possible are removed." [August]
checks.page_wording: Ensure rose prunings and as many fallen leaves as possible are removed.
checks.note: Under August heading, South Australia. Supports clearing leaves and prunings, but names August only, not July to August; the July entry has no such sentence.

checks.recorded: "After tidying up, ensure roses are sprayed with Winter Oil (or pest oil) or Lime Sulphur" [August]
checks.page_wording: After tidying up, ensure roses are sprayed with Winter Oil (or pest oil) or Lime Sulphur.
checks.note: Under August heading, South Australia. Supports the South Australian August winter spray after tidying; spray types named are oil (winter/pest oil) or lime sulphur.

contradictions: No sentence gives a frost or cold-area delay; the calendar is purely by month for South Australia.

also_says.quote: New roses will arrive and can be planted...Ensure they are removed from plastic, soaked in a bucket of water for 12 hours.
also_says.note: June heading, South Australia; bare-root planting in June.

also_says.quote: Earlier flowering cultivars should have their spent blooms removed by taking the dead flower and around 15cm of stem down to the second five leaflet.
also_says.note: November heading, South Australia; deadheading method; page gives no stop date.

also_says.quote: The outer canes should be reduced to one-third to half of their original height.
also_says.note: July heading, South Australia; pruning method, not timing.

checks.recorded: "Pruning in July is recommended and avoid the temptation to prune too early."
checks.page_wording: Pruning in July is recommended and avoid the temptation to prune too early.
checks.note: Rose Society of South Australia winter notes, South Australia (Adelaide baseline). Supports July for the main winter pruning; no frost or region exception given for pruning.

checks.recorded: [No sentence timing pruning by bud swell or new growth; checked directly.]
checks.note: Asked directly twice: the page times pruning by the month (July) and does not mention bud swell or new growth. Absence supports the finding for this South Australian page. Not a quotation, so there is nothing to confirm.

checks.recorded: "Planting is best done in June, July or early August."
checks.page_wording: Planting is best done in June, July or early August.
checks.note: South Australia. Supports June and July but the window also runs to early August; the sentence says 'Planting' and the page's following material is about bare-root, so applies to bare-root only by context.

checks.recorded: "Planting is best done in June, July or early August."
checks.page_wording: Planting is best done in June, July or early August.
checks.note: South Australia. Supports an August extension (early August) for planting; says nothing about May or Canberra.

checks.recorded: "Winter is the best time to transplant existing roses."
checks.page_wording: Winter is the best time to transplant existing roses. This can be easily done until the rose is about 10 years old.
checks.note: South Australia. Supports winter as the time to move an established rose; the sentence does not say 'dormant' and names no month.

checks.recorded: "most of the fallen leaves are gathered up and disposed of together with any discarded rose prunings"
checks.page_wording: Once roses lose their leaves and assuming most of the fallen leaves are gathered up and disposed of together with discarded rose prunings, winter is a great time for pest and disease control.
checks.note: South Australia. Page says leaves and prunings are gathered up, as a precondition for winter pest and disease spraying; it names winter generally, not July to August. Recorded fragment is slightly reworded ('any discarded').

checks.recorded: "colder and wetter in the Adelaide Hills ... Frosts are also common in country areas."
checks.page_wording: colder and wetter in the Adelaide Hills, the South-East and Southern Yorke Peninsula and Eyre Peninsula. Frosts are also common in country areas.
checks.note: South Australia. Supports that conditions differ within the state (Adelaide vs Hills, South-East, Yorke and Eyre Peninsulas, country areas); it does not say timing changes, nor go down to neighbouring suburbs. The ellipsis joins two sentences.

contradictions: The page's pruning advice is July with no August or frost delay, unlike the same society's Rose Growing Guide (RSSA-GG) which says August in frost areas.

also_says.quote: they can readily be treated with winter dormancy sprays, for example oil sprays or Lime Sulphur.
also_says.note: South Australia; winter generally, no month given; type: oil or lime sulphur.

also_says.quote: Copper Oxy Chloride sprays can also be used.
also_says.note: South Australia; winter; copper type; no month.

checks.recorded: "If an application of Sudden Impact for Roses was not applied in February, ensure the rose plants receive it in March."
checks.page_wording: If an application of Sudden Impact for Roses was not applied in February, ensure the rose plants receive it in March.
checks.note: Fertilising section, South Australia (publisher's state). Supports a feed in February to March in autumn notes; names a brand product. Page also says a liquid fertiliser is applied fortnightly until the end of March, consistent with March as the last feed.

checks.recorded: "A light, late summer or early autumn trim will ensure a great flush of flowers around 55 days later."
checks.page_wording: A light, late summer or early autumn trim will ensure a great flush of flowers around 55 days later.
checks.note: Flowering section, South Australia. Supports a light trim in late summer or early autumn timed for autumn flowers (55 days); it names no months, so the January to March range is not stated here.

contradictions: Finding AF-22 says February to March; page says liquid feed continues until the end of March, so March is the last feed for South Australia.

also_says.quote: Sudden Impact for Roses Liquid Fertiliser applied in fortnightly applications until the end of March
also_says.note: Fertilising section, South Australia; last feed end of March.

also_says.quote: apply a preventative organic oil or fungicide spray mid to late April to ensure plants remain clean
also_says.note: Pests and Diseases section, South Australia; mid to late April; type: organic oil or fungicide; this is an autumn preventative spray, not the winter dormancy spray.

also_says.quote: If you want to purchase bare root roses in winter, it's time to order them now.
also_says.note: South Australia; autumn; ordering only, planting is in winter.

also_says.quote: Look at the forward weather forecast for the next 7 days
also_says.note: South Australia; autumn; used to decide watering, not pruning or feeding timing.

checks.recorded: "be applied when the young shoots are around 2cms in length."
checks.page_wording: It is recommended that Neutrog 'Sudden Impact for Roses' be applied when the young shoots are around 2cms in length.
checks.note: South Australia (publisher's state). Supports tying the first spring feed to a growth stage (young shoots about 2 cm) rather than a month; the page gives no month for it.

checks.recorded: "mid to late October in warmer areas, including Adelaide, and in early to mid-November in cooler areas of the State"
checks.page_wording: The first flush of flowers can be expected in mid to late October in warmer areas, including Adelaide, and in early to mid-November in cooler areas.
checks.note: South Australia. The sentence is about when the first flowers appear, not about timing of tasks; it supports regional variation within the state (warmer areas incl. Adelaide vs cooler areas) but not suburb-level variation or that task timing changes.

also_says.quote: Natural oil sprays, such as Eco Oil, and milk spray are great 'gentle on the environment', preventative sprays.
also_says.note: South Australia; spring preventative spray (oil or milk), not a winter spray; no month.

also_says.quote: If blooms are one per stem, the old bloom and a portion of stem down to second five-leaflet leaf is recommended to be removed.
also_says.note: South Australia; spring deadheading method; no stop date.

checks.recorded: "Pruning is best done in July (or August in frost areas)."
checks.page_wording: Pruning is best done in July (or August in frost areas).
checks.note: Rose Society of South Australia guide, South Australia. Supports July for the main winter pruning, with August for frost areas.

checks.recorded: "Pruning is best done in July (or August in frost areas)."
checks.page_wording: Pruning is best done in July (or August in frost areas).
checks.note: South Australia. Supports August delay in frost areas for South Australia only; says nothing about NSW inland, Victoria or Canberra, and does not say 'cold' or 'inland'.

checks.recorded: "early September and February in heavy soil"
checks.page_wording: Fertiliser is best applied twice over a 12 month period - early September and February in heavy soil
checks.note: South Australia, heavy soil. Supports early September as the first spring feed (heavy soil; sandy soils also start in September), but not late August. Fragment omits the leading words 'twice over a 12 month period'.

checks.recorded: "four times a year in September, November, February and April in sandy soils"
checks.page_wording: four times a year in September, November, February and April in sandy soils
checks.note: South Australia, sandy soils only. Supports an April last feed in sandy soils in South Australia; does not cover Western Australia or May.

checks.recorded: "This is best done in June or July."
checks.page_wording: This is best done in June or July.
checks.note: South Australia; under planting winter bare-rooted roses. Supports June and July for bare-root planting there.

checks.recorded: "After pruning, spray with Pest Oil, Winter Oil or Copper Oxychloride to combat overwintering fungal spores."
checks.page_wording: After pruning, spray with Pest Oil, Winter Oil or Copper Oxychloride to combat overwintering fungal spores
checks.note: South Australia; in the pruning section. Supports a spray after pruning (types: oil or copper); no month given for the spray, so July vs August is only implied by the pruning months (July, or August in frost areas).

contradictions: AF-19 says late August or September; this guide says early September (and September in sandy soils), with no August start.

also_says.quote: Remove dead flowers and hips with a short stem as if picking a bunch of flowers.
also_says.note: South Australia; method only; no stop date.

also_says.quote: Fertiliser is best applied twice over a 12 month period - early September and February in heavy soil
also_says.note: South Australia; feeding schedule varies with soil type (heavy: twice, sandy: four times) rather than climate zone.

checks.recorded: "Remember don't plant in hot weather."
checks.page_wording: Remember don't plant in hot weather.
checks.note: South Australia (publisher's state). Sits in the container-choice section of a page on roses grown in pots; it supports only the 'avoid hot weather' half. The page does not say potted roses can be planted at any time of year; asked directly, it said no such statement exists. Page metadata shows image dates of 2026-09-12, not a page date.

contradictions: The page does not say potted roses can be planted all year; it only advises against hot weather. It also says repotting is done when dormant, every 3 to 5 years.

also_says.quote: Roses should be repotted with new soil, when dormant, every 3 to 5 years.
also_says.note: South Australia; container roses; dormant (winter) repotting, no months.

also_says.quote: An occasional spray with Eco-oil or pest oil will control fungal problems and help with insect control.
also_says.note: South Australia; container roses; oil type; not a winter spray, no month.

checks.recorded: "Prune to suit your flowering goals, remove inward-growing shoots." [WINTER (June - July)]
checks.page_wording: Prune to suit your flowering goals, remove inward-growing shoots.
checks.note: Rose Society of Western Australia calendar, Western Australia (no sub-region). Under the heading WINTER (June - July), so pruning is placed from June; the sentence itself names no month.

checks.recorded: "Feed as new growth appears and apply mulch." [EARLY SPRING (August - September)]
checks.page_wording: Feed as new growth appears and apply mulch.
checks.note: Western Australia. Under EARLY SPRING (August - September): supports spring feeding starting in August to September, but tied to new growth rather than a month; the finding's 'late August or September' is narrower than the heading.

checks.recorded: "Feed as new growth appears and apply mulch."
checks.page_wording: Feed as new growth appears and apply mulch.
checks.note: Western Australia. Supports tying the first spring feed to growth appearing, not to a pruning date.

checks.recorded: "Continue feeding and deadheading." [LATE AUTUMN (May)]
checks.page_wording: Continue feeding and deadheading.
checks.note: Western Australia. Under LATE AUTUMN (May): supports feeding continuing into May. The page does not call it the last feed, but no feeding is listed for June to July.

checks.recorded: "Light summer prune (about one-third) to encourage fresh growth." [EARLY AUTUMN (March - April)]
checks.page_wording: Light summer prune (about one-third) to encourage fresh growth.
checks.note: Western Australia. The page places the light summer prune in March to April (heading EARLY AUTUMN), later than the finding's January to March, and says the aim is fresh growth, not timing autumn flowers.

checks.recorded: "Continue feeding and deadheading." [LATE AUTUMN (May)]
checks.page_wording: Continue feeding and deadheading.
checks.note: Western Australia. Deadheading is listed through May (and again Nov-Dec); the page gives no month to stop. Supports that some sources continue deadheading into May.

checks.recorded: "Plant new roses for future seasons of colour." [LATE AUTUMN (May)]
checks.page_wording: Plant new roses for future seasons of colour.
checks.note: Western Australia. Under LATE AUTUMN (May): supports planting new roses in May, but does not say bare-root; the June to July heading separately says 'Plant or repot roses as needed'.

checks.recorded: "Spray after pruning to clean up pests and disease." [WINTER (June - July)]
checks.page_wording: Spray after pruning to clean up pests and disease.
checks.note: Western Australia. Under WINTER (June - July): supports a post-pruning spray in June to July. The page names no spray type.
